body: Cox & Kings, a 250-year-old travel brand, defaulted on commercial paper on 26 Jun 2019; the stock fell sharply within two days and went to ~Rs 2-3 from ~Rs 250-400 levels of 2015-18. Lenders' claims ~Rs 5,500 cr in insolvency. A lender-appointed PwC audit found ~Rs 4,367 cr siphoned and books manipulated from Apr 2014 to Jun 2019 to obtain bank credit; foreign subsidiaries (e.g., Prometheon) allegedly forged reports of global audit firms and bank statements, which were then consolidated by Indian auditors. Visible flags: (1) a 'travel' business that should be working-capital-positive carried heavy and rising debt; (2) large receivables and loans/advances despite customers paying in advance; (3) CFO persistently weak relative to reported profit; (4) debt-funded 2011 Holidaybreak (UK) acquisition and complex offshore holding chains; (5) consolidated accounts relying on subsidiaries audited by other firms; (6) high promoter pledges and dependence on CP and Yes Bank lending. Lesson: when a business model implies negative working capital but the balance sheet shows high receivables and debt, the accounts are wrong. Offshore subsidiaries audited by different firms are a soft spot in consolidation.

data.early_signals: debt + receivables in an advance-paid business; weak CFO; complex offshore subs; pledges; CP dependence
data.lesson: Business model should predict the working-capital sign; mismatch = red flag

title: Cox & Kings: forged foreign-subsidiary books (2019)
